design_detail: Critical analysis in the history and philosophy of science. The authors outline a feminist philosophy of science framework (science embedded in the communities that produce it; methods built on men; men's experience treated as the universal standard) and apply it to selected 'key source publications' on telescoping: Jellinek's surveys of Alcoholics Anonymous members (1946, 1952), the 1952 WHO expert committee report, Lisansky (1958), James (1975), Mulford (1977), Piazza et al. (1986, 1989), and later studies of other drugs and gambling. Includes a count of the articles citing Piazza et al. (1989) in Web of Science and PubMed, and one figure redrawn from Piazza et al. (1989). No search strategy, inclusion criteria, appraisal tool or quantitative synthesis.
can_establish: Where the telescoping idea came from (stage models built from recalled drinking histories of men in Alcoholics Anonymous, with women's data set aside), how small and clinically selected the samples were in which it was first described, how often the 1989 paper is cited as a general rationale rather than tested, and the conceptual objections to making men the reference group.
cannot_establish: Whether women's drinking or drug use actually progresses faster than men's (the empirical studies are neither searched for systematically nor appraised nor pooled); whether any biological or social mechanism produces such a difference (the authors say none has been demonstrated); or whether abandoning the term would improve research or care (a normative proposal, not a tested one).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (critical narrative review). The studies discussed are described with their samples: Jellinek's mailed questionnaire to Alcoholics Anonymous members (98 men analysed); James's mailed questionnaire to women in Alcoholics Anonymous (89 women); Mulford's patients at Iowa community alcoholism centres (3,132 men, 395 women); Piazza's women in residential treatment and Alcoholics Anonymous (41 women, 1986) and people from treatment programmes and self-help groups (33 women, 105 men, 1989); and a national sample of 1,217 women and 3,297 men for cannabis (Khan et al., 2013; a NESARC general-population analysis by its reference title) (History of Telescoping Research).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated; the authors chose the publications, described in the abstract as drawn from international and US peer-reviewed journals published from 1952 onwards (the text also uses Jellinek's 1946 survey).
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the authors' own and serves the conceptual argument. Nearly all the foundational evidence comes from treatment programmes and self-help groups, where people who reach treatment are, by construction, the people being timed; the authors state that the progressive-disease model behind telescoping leaves out people who recover without treatment or return to non-problem drinking.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level. In the studies described, landmark ages (first drink, first drunkenness, first alcohol-related problem, first treatment admission) were recalled by people in treatment or self-help groups and reported in questionnaires; none is described as recorded as it happened. The review does not say what, if anything, the later studies adjusted for.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed, apart from James's (1975) questions on the timing of tranquilizer use relative to drinking.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (James's respondents reported a mean of three years' continuous abstinence, range 1–19).

comparison.controls: The paper's central point: in telescoping research men are the reference group and women are compared on landmarks defined from men's drinking histories.

outcomes.instruments: As described for the cited studies: Jellinek's 36-item questionnaire mailed through the AA Grapevine; the Iowa Alcoholic Intake Schedule, validated among men (Mulford); James's women-specific questionnaire (39 items from Jellinek and Glatt plus 85 written from recovering women's experiences); Piazza's questionnaire on landmark ages.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors' critique is that landmarks, criteria and instruments were developed and validated in men and then applied to women.
outcomes.operationalization: Telescoping as described by Piazza et al. (1989): a later onset of drinking in women but a shorter interval from landmark to landmark, especially from first alcohol-related problem to first treatment.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited, none pooled. Piazza et al. (1989): women began drinking about 2 years later and first became intoxicated about 3 years later than men, entered treatment at the same age, and had a mean interval from first problem to first treatment 4.3 years shorter. Mulford (1977): women arrived for treatment about 2 years after their first attempt to quit, men about 3 years. Khan et al. (2013): time from first cannabis use to cannabis use disorder 2.5 years shorter in women. Citation count: 75 of 103 articles citing Piazza et al. (1989) used telescoping only as a rationale.
analysis.selective_reporting: The empirical studies for and against telescoping receive one paragraph; methodological explanations other than gender bias (recalled onset ages; who reaches treatment and when) are not discussed. Biological sex differences in alcohol effects are presented with single citations as possible mechanisms, without appraisal.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A historical account showing that the stage model behind telescoping came from recalled drinking histories of men in Alcoholics Anonymous (98 men analysed by Jellinek, 15 women set aside), that the 1989 telescoping paper rested on 33 women and 105 men from treatment and self-help settings, that later and larger samples, including a general-population analysis of alcohol, gave discrepant results, while a national general-population survey of cannabis use disorder (NESARC, by its reference title) is described as finding a 2.5-year shorter interval in women, and that most papers citing the 1989 study use it as background rather than test it.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The authors conclude that telescoping research carried gender bias in its conventions, methods and language, and that the term "telescoping" and the "masculine" framework "should be discarded" (Conclusions, 3rd paragraph). This is a normative recommendation drawn from a conceptual and historical critique, and the paper presents it as such. Gaps: (1) the argument about biased origins does not by itself show that the timing difference is absent; the empirical question is handled in one paragraph that cites studies on both sides without appraising them; (2) the statement that telescoping may occur only in people who go on to a clinical diagnosis is attributed to the general-population analysis of Keyes et al. (2010) but not examined; (3) biological differences (body water, alcohol metabolism, liver disease, heart disease, brain atrophy in women) are presented as possible mechanisms on single citations, beside the authors' own statement that no mechanism has been demonstrated; (4) the claim that the victim narrative was clinically counterproductive is put as a possibility without evidence.

timeline.event: Jellinek's analysis of a questionnaire mailed through the AA Grapevine: about 10% response, 98 men analysed, 15 women excluded as too few and too different (as described by Marks and Clark).
WHO expert committee report: phases of alcoholism in women less clear-cut and development often more rapid (as quoted by Marks and Clark).
Lisansky first uses the phrase 'telescoped development' for women's alcoholism (as described by Marks and Clark).
James's women-specific questionnaire (89 women in Alcoholics Anonymous; 29 with complete data): 8 of 26 Jellinek symptoms at a different stage in women (as described by Marks and Clark).
Mulford, Iowa community alcoholism centres (3,132 men, 395 women): women reached treatment sooner after a first attempt to quit (as described by Marks and Clark).
Piazza, Vrbka and Yeager define telescoping in 33 women and 105 men from treatment programmes and self-help groups (as described by Marks and Clark).
Project MATCH treatment-sample study, placed by Marks and Clark among studies with discrepant results (see reporting issues).
General-population analysis of two US surveys finds no full telescoping pattern.
National cannabis analysis (Khan et al., 2013; a NESARC general-population survey by its reference title): time to cannabis use disorder 2.5 years shorter in women (as described by Marks and Clark).
This critique recommends discarding the term telescoping.

replication.where_it_stands: A conceptual critique, not an empirical test. It documents that the telescoping construct was built on men's recalled histories in clinical and self-help samples and that the general-population test for alcohol did not find the full pattern, while it describes a general-population survey of cannabis use disorder (Khan et al., 2013; NESARC by its reference title; timing measure and adjustment not given) as finding a shorter time in women; it does not settle whether progression differs by sex. The review by McHugh et al. (2018) is the broader evidence summary on this round's list.

funding.funder: Role of Funding Source: National Institute on Drug Abuse, T32 DA035200 to K.R. Marks; the funder had no role in design, data collection or analysis, or preparation and submission of the manuscript (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors have no conflict of interest to declare (Footnotes).
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors: Department of Behavioral Science, University of Kentucky. Clark is a co-author of one cited qualitative study (Cooper et al., 2014); no other reliance on the authors' own work.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic review of telescoping studies that separates treatment samples from general-population samples and recalled from prospectively recorded timing; and a prospective general-population cohort, designed from the start to test sex and gender differences in course, with landmarks and measures validated in both women and men and analysed by race, class and age as well as gender.

domains.note: Key publications chosen by the authors; no search strategy, dates or criteria, apart from an undated citation count in Web of Science and PubMed.

Samples, response rates and the male basis of the instruments are described for the historical studies, but the empirical tests of telescoping (Piazza 1989, Khan 2013, Keyes 2010 and others) are not appraised for recall of onset ages or for selection into treatment.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: One cited study has a co-author of this review (Cooper et al., 2014).

The recommendation to discard the term is clearly normative, and the authors say no mechanism has been demonstrated; but biological mechanisms are listed on single citations and the clinical harm of the victim narrative is asserted without evidence.

domains.domain: Balance between the conceptual critique and the empirical evidence on timing
domains.note: Studies that found telescoping and studies that did not each get a sentence; explanations other than gender bias (recalled onset ages, timing of treatment entry) are under-represented.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist gives high, set by the absence of a systematic search. The review is useful and explicit about its aim: it may be cited for the history of the concept (Jellinek's male AA samples, the exclusion of women's data, the small treatment and self-help sample of 1989), for the argument that men were the reference group, and for the observation that most citing papers use telescoping as a rationale. It should not be cited as evidence that telescoping does or does not occur; the primary studies, read directly, carry that question.

key_findings.finding: Jellinek's stage model came from a 36-item questionnaire mailed to Alcoholics Anonymous members through the AA Grapevine in about 1945: about 10% responded, data were analysed for 98 men, and the 15 women's data were excluded as too few and too different from the men's (the differences were not specified). The later replication in over 2,000 participants was also confined to men in Alcoholics Anonymous. Ages at each point were recalled.
key_findings.locator: History of Telescoping Research › Foundational Background, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: A 1952 WHO expert committee report described the phases of alcoholism in women as less clear-cut and their development as often more rapid; Lisansky used the phrase 'telescoped development' in 1958 and warned that stereotypes could shape research on women's drinking.
key_findings.locator: History of Telescoping Research › Foundational Background, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Mulford (1977), a treatment sample from Iowa community alcoholism service centres (3,132 men, 395 women), using an interview validated among men: women arrived for treatment about two years after their first attempt to quit drinking, men about three years.
key_findings.locator: History of Telescoping Research › Empirical Research, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: James (1975) built a women-specific questionnaire (39 items from Jellinek and Glatt plus 85 written from recovering women's experiences) and mailed it through the AA Grapevine: 15% response, 89 women, mean age about 45, mean continuous abstinence 3 years (range 1–19). In the 29 women with complete data, 8 of the 26 Jellinek symptoms fell at a different stage than in Jellinek's men; the comparison was descriptive, not statistical.
key_findings.locator: History of Telescoping Research › Empirical Research, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Piazza et al. (1986) re-analysed 18 Jellinek symptoms in 41 women from residential treatment and Alcoholics Anonymous and concluded that Jellinek's model described women's alcoholism; the women-specific questions were not used.
key_findings.locator: History of Telescoping Research › Empirical Research, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Piazza et al. (1989), widely credited with defining the term telescoping (the phrase 'telescoped development' had been used by Lisansky in 1958; key finding 1): 33 women and 105 men recruited from treatment programmes and self-help groups answered a questionnaire on ages at first drink, first drunkenness, first alcohol-related problem and first treatment admission (recalled). Men and women entered treatment at the same age; women started drinking about 2 years later and were first intoxicated about 3 years later; the mean interval from first problem to first treatment was 4.3 years shorter in women, who reported as many symptoms over a shorter time.
key_findings.locator: History of Telescoping Research › Empirical Research, 5th paragraph; Figure 1 (redrawn from Piazza et al., 1989)
key_findings.note: Figure 1 is an image; a screenshot of the tab came back blank, so the figure image was not viewable and no values were read from it.

key_findings.finding: Similar findings were reported for other drugs and gambling; for example, in a national sample of 1,217 women and 3,297 men, time from first cannabis use to cannabis use disorder was 2.5 years shorter in women (Khan et al., 2013). Larger and more diverse samples gave discrepant results, with fewer telescoping effects in some cohorts; the authors summarize Keyes et al. (2010) as finding no telescoping in the general population and suggest it may occur only in people who go on to a clinical diagnosis. They state that the mechanism has not been demonstrated.
key_findings.locator: History of Telescoping Research › Empirical Research, 6th paragraph
key_findings.note: The reference list gives Khan et al. (2013) as a NESARC analysis of gender differences in cannabis use disorders (Drug and Alcohol Dependence 130:101–108), that is, a US general-population survey; the text says only that participants were recruited nationally, and gives no timing measure or adjustment.

key_findings.finding: Of 103 peer-reviewed articles citing Piazza et al. (1989) in a Web of Science and PubMed search, 75 did not study telescoping but cited it as a rationale or context for sex and gender differences in general.
key_findings.locator: History of Telescoping Research › Empirical Research, 7th paragraph
key_findings.note: The date of the citation search is not given.

key_findings.finding: Proposed biological mechanisms (hormones, metabolism, subjective drug effects) and social ones (stronger social consequences and disapproval for women, the role of mothers, partners' drug use and loss of a partner) are listed; the authors state that a causal relation between any of them and telescoping has not been demonstrated.
key_findings.locator: History of Telescoping Research › Empirical Research, 8th and 9th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors identify gender bias in three places: the progressive-disease conventions drawn from male AA convenience samples, which leave out people who recover without treatment; landmarks, criteria and instruments validated in men, with men as the reference group (had women been the reference, men's longer course might have been called 'magnification'); and comparative language such as 'accelerated progression' and 'a more severe form of alcoholism'.

Recommendations: discard the term telescoping and the 'masculine' framework; design studies from the outset to test sex and gender differences rather than run underpowered post hoc comparisons; describe group differences in descriptive rather than comparative language; and study how sex and gender intersect with race, class, age, education and culture.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions › Feminist Philosophy as a Transformative Framework for Future Directions, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The text says Piazza et al. (1989) was published in International Journal of Mental Health and Addiction; the abstract, the introduction and the reference list give The International Journal of the Addictions.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), History of Telescoping Research › Empirical Research, 5th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite Piazza et al. (1989) from the reference list entry, not the text.

reporting_issues.issue: Citation slips: 'Jellinek, 19452' in the text; Lisansky's name spelled Lisansky, Linsansky and Liansky; Campbell and Wasco cited as 2000 in the text and 2010 in the reference list; Hankivsky and 'Cromier' 2008 in the text against Hankivsky and Cormier 2009; Rounsaville spelled Rousanville. The abstract says the publications examined date from 1952, but the analysis starts from Jellinek's 1946 report.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), History of Telescoping Research › Foundational Background, 1st, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Conclusions, 3rd paragraph; References
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; secondary details should be traced to the primary sources by DOI.

reporting_issues.issue: Jellinek is said to have identified 43 symptoms from a 36-item questionnaire, and James's comparison is against 26 Jellinek symptoms; the counts are not reconciled.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), History of Telescoping Research › Foundational Background, 1st paragraph; History of Telescoping Research › Empirical Research, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Numbers of Jellinek's symptoms should be taken from the primary reports, not from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: Randall et al. (1999) is listed among larger samples with discrepant results and fewer telescoping effects, whereas Keyes et al. (2010) cite the same study as showing faster progression to dependence and to treatment in women.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), History of Telescoping Research › Empirical Research, 6th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Two papers on this round's list characterize randall_1999 differently; the primary paper must be read before either description is used.

reporting_issues.issue: Lower total body water and slower alcohol metabolism in women are attributed to Frezza et al. (1990), whose title, as given in the reference list, concerns gastric alcohol dehydrogenase and first-pass metabolism.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), History of Telescoping Research › Empirical Research, 8th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The body-water statement does not match the cited source as titled; claims about sex differences in alcohol handling should rest on the pharmacokinetic studies themselves.
